t: The Hussites followed the reformer Jan Hus, burned at the stake at the Council of Constance on 6 July 1415, and took the chalice of wine given to the laity as their emblem.

They were not one movement but several parties: moderate Utraquists, who wished to leave the order of the Church untouched, and radical Taborites, Orebites and Orphans, who held to Wycliffe’s teaching and wished to remove the hierarchy.

After the crusades and civil wars of the Hussite Wars (1420–1434) the Utraquists came out dominant, Catholics and Utraquists were given legal equality in 1485, and Roman Catholicism was reimposed in Bohemia only after the Battle of White Mountain in 1620.
dyk: The name Tábor was a play on words: in Czech it meant a camp or encampment, and it was also the traditional name of the mountain on which Jesus was expected to return.
ev: Jan Hus is tried for heresy by the Council of Constance and burned at the stake
News of the death of King Wenceslaus produces a revolution in Prague: churches and monasteries are destroyed and church property seized
The Four Articles of Prague, written by Jacob of Mies, set out the programme of the moderate Hussites
A Bohemian–Moravian assembly in Prague accepts the Compactata, granting communion in both kinds
The Calixtines and Catholics together destroy the Taborites at the Battle of Lipany
The Diet of Kutná Hora makes an agreement between Catholics and Utraquists
The Battle of White Mountain opens the way for the reimposition of Roman Catholicism
A settlement of Hussites at Herrnhut in Saxony leads to the emergence of the Moravian Church

f.where: the Kingdom of Bohemia and the other Lands of the Bohemian Crown, including Moravia and Silesia; inroads into the north of the Kingdom of Hungary (now Slovakia); small temporary communities in Poland-Lithuania and Transylvania; later refuge communities in Lissa (Leszno), the Low Countries and Herrnhut in Saxony
f.period: organised 1415–1419; Four Articles of Prague 1420; Hussite Wars 1420–1434; Compactata of Prague 1433; Battle of Lipany 1434; religious peace of Kutná Hora 1485; Catholicism reimposed after White Mountain 1620; Herrnhut settlement 1722; Czechoslovak Hussite Church after 1918
f.figures: Jan Hus, the reformer executed in 1415; Jan Žižka, Taborite leader who resisted five crusades; Jacob of Mies, author of the Four Articles; Jerome of Prague, a major theologian; Petr Chelčický, pacifist whose teachings underlay the Unitas Fratrum; Jan Amos Comenius, who fled to the Low Countries
f.outcome: the moderate Utraquists became the dominant Hussite group in Bohemia and the Taborites were defeated in 1434; Catholics and Utraquists had legal equality from 1485; Catholicism was reimposed after 1620; the tradition continues in the Moravian Church, the Unity of the Brethren and the Czechoslovak Hussite Church
